In `contextmanager_in_threadpool`, `__enter__` runs through the normal shared threadpool. `__exit__` is run with `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` using a fresh `CapacityLimiter(1)` created for that call. Teardown therefore never queues behind the global thread limit, so it can't deadlock when every worker is busy, for example on a database connection pool. `fastapi/dependencies/utils.py` (line 585) wraps sync `yield` dependencies in this helper.

In `fastapi/routing.py`, the request handler reads the body bytes and then looks at the `Content-Type` header. If the header is missing, it decodes the body as JSON only when `strict_content_type` is `False`. With the default `True`, the body stays as raw bytes. If the header is present, it is parsed with `email.message.Message`. The body is decoded as JSON when the main type is `application` and the subtype is `json` or ends in `+json`. Any other content type leaves the body as raw bytes. `fastapi/applications.py` only exposes the `strict_content_type` option and passes it down to the router.

**Nesting order, outermost to innermost:** `ServerErrorMiddleware`, then the user-registered middleware, then `ExceptionMiddleware`, then `AsyncExitStackMiddleware`, then the router (the request dispatcher). `build_middleware_stack` in `fastapi/applications.py` builds this list and wraps the router in reverse order.

**Why the file-closing layer is innermost:** `AsyncExitStackMiddleware` sits inside all the user middlewares because they create a new contextvars context through an anyio task group. Placing the exit stack inside them keeps it in the same context as the request handling, so contextvars set while handling the request are visible when it closes the files. The comments in `build_middleware_stack` say this is not strictly needed now that dependencies with `yield` have their own exit stack.

`FastAPI.build_middleware_stack` nests the layers from outermost to innermost as `ServerErrorMiddleware`, then the user-registered middlewares, then `ExceptionMiddleware`, then `AsyncExitStackMiddleware` (the layer that closes uploaded files), and finally the router, which does the dispatching. The file-closing layer sits innermost, inside all user middlewares, because user middlewares run in a new AnyIO task group and so get a copy of the contextvars context. Keeping its `AsyncExitStack` in that same inner context means contextvars set while handling the request stay visible to it, as they would have been when it also closed `yield` dependencies. It also closes the files only after the endpoint and response are finished.
